meta.title: Ballet 1830–1930
meta.description: Offline reference app: 48 cross-linked entries on ballet history from 1830 to 1930 — 20 ballets, 10 dancers, 6 impresarios & choreographers, 6 theatres, 6 composers.

entries.title: La Sylphide
entries.dates: Premiered 8 March 1832, Salle Le Peletier, Paris Opéra
entries.history: The landmark of Romantic ballet. Filippo Taglioni created it for his daughter Marie Taglioni, who danced the title role en pointe, and the premiere made her the idol of the Paris Opéra. Music by Jean-Madeleine Schneitzhoeffer; libretto by Adolphe Nourrit. August Bournonville later made his own celebrated 1836 version in Copenhagen with music by Herman Løvenskiold.
entries.synopsis: A Scottish lord, James, is visited on his wedding eve by a Sylph (air spirit) he loves. He abandons his fiancée for her, only to discover she is mortal-bound; the sorceress Madge's curse destroys the Sylph and James is left alone.

entries.title: Giselle
entries.dates: Premiered 28 June 1841, Salle Le Peletier, Paris Opéra
entries.history: The supreme Romantic ballet, created by Jean Coralli and Jules Perrot for Carlotta Grisi, with music by Adolphe Adam and a libretto by Théophile Gautier. It remains one of the most performed ballets in the world and defined the ballerina's dual role — village girl by day, vengeful spirit by night.
entries.synopsis: The peasant Giselle falls in love with Albrecht, who is secretly a nobleman engaged to another. Discovering the betrayal, she dies of a broken heart; her spirit joins the Wilis, ghosts of jilted brides who dance men to death, but she saves Albrecht from their queen Myrtha.

image.credit: The original uploader was Mrlopez2681 at English Wikipedia.

entries.title: La Esmeralda
entries.dates: Premiered 9 March 1844, Her Majesty's Theatre, London
entries.history: Jules Perrot's spectacular Romantic ballet to a score by Cesare Pugni, based on Victor Hugo's novel Notre-Dame de Paris. It was a great success in London and became a standard vehicle for the era's leading ballerinas.
entries.synopsis: The beggar girl Esmeralda is loved by the hunchback bell-ringer Quasimodo and desired by the corrupt priest Frollo. When she is condemned to hang, Quasimodo rescues her, but she is mortally wounded; he dies beside her in Notre-Dame.

image.commonsTitle: File:Charles-Antoine Cambon - La Esmeralda, Act 3, Scene 2 set.jpg

entries.title: Pas de Quatre
entries.dates: Premiered 12 July 1845, Her Majesty's Theatre, London
entries.history: Jules Perrot gathered the four greatest ballerinas of the age — Marie Taglioni, Carlotta Grisi, Lucile Grahn and Fanny Cerrito — for this one-act ballet to music by Cesare Pugni, commissioned for Queen Victoria's birthday. It was the sensation of the 1845 London season.
entries.synopsis: Four rival ballerinas meet in a dreamlike allegory and dance together in a celebrated coda; there is no plot, only pure dance display.

entries.title: Le Corsaire
entries.dates: Premiered 17 January 1856, Paris Opéra (Salle Le Peletier)
entries.history: Joseph Mazilier's swashbuckling ballet, created after Jules Perrot, with music by Adolphe Adam and a scenario from Byron's poem The Corsair. Famous for its grand pas de deux and the 'Le Corsaire' pas, it was a staple of the Paris Opéra for a century.
entries.synopsis: The pirate Conrad loves Medora, a slave in the harem of the pacha Said. With his fellow corsairs he raids the seraglio, frees the women and defeats Said, winning Medora.

image.commonsTitle: File:"Le Corsaire". Ballet-pantomime en 3 actes et 5 tableaux, musique d'Adolphe Adam, livret de Saint-Georges, chorégraphie de Mazilier. Création à l'Opéra de la rue Le Peletier le 23 janvier 1856 - btv1b525149996 (099 of 478).jpg

entries.title: The Daughter of Pharaoh
entries.dates: Premiered 1862, Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow
entries.history: Marius Petipa's first great Russian success, to music by Cesare Pugni, staged for the Bolshoi Theatre. Its spectacular Egyptomania — elephants, lions, a lion-taming scene — made it a template for the grand Russian ballet.
entries.synopsis: The English lord John Wilson falls in love with Aspicia, daughter of the Pharaoh, and is nearly sacrificed to a crocodile before the river Nile floods and saves him; he wakes to find it was all a dream induced by opium.

image.credit: Unknown photographer of the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre. St. Petersburg, Russian Empire.

entries.title: Don Quixote
entries.dates: Premiered 18 December 1869, Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow
entries.history: Petipa's comic ballet to Ludwig Minkus's score, based loosely on Cervantes. Its bravura variations for the innkeeper's daughter Kitri became a fixture of every ballerina's repertoire. Petipa later restaged it at the Mariinsky in 1871.
entries.synopsis: Don Quixote, dreaming of his Dulcinea, arrives at an inn where the landlord's daughter Kitri loves the barber Basilio. Quixote helps the lovers unite and jousts with windmills in comic pantomime.

image.credit: Theatrical Artwork by Laura Fiorucci. Picture by  Wilfredor
image.commonsTitle: File:Ballet Don Quijote en Teatro Teresa Carreño 3.jpg

entries.title: Coppélia
entries.dates: Premiered 25 May 1870, Paris Opéra (Salle Le Peletier)
entries.history: Arthur Saint-Léon's comic masterpiece to Léo Delibes's charming score, based on E. T. A. Hoffmann's tale Der Sandmann, with Giuseppina Bozzini as Swanilda. It is the last great ballet of the Romantic era and still opens every season at the Paris Opéra.
entries.synopsis: The toy-maker Coppélius has built a lifelike doll, Coppélia. Franz falls in love with her, not knowing she is a doll; Swanilda, his fiancée, disguises herself as the doll and brings Franz back to her.

image.credit:
Photography studio of the Théâtre Impérial de l´Opéra. Paris, France.

〔Original uploader was Mrlopez2681 at en.wikipedia〕

entries.title: Le Carnaval
entries.dates: Premiered 1873, Paris Opéra (Salle Le Peletier)
entries.history: Saint-Léon's festive ballet to music by Léo Delibes, a series of dances evoking the Venetian carnival — Harlequin, Pierrot, Columbine and the butterfly. It charmed Paris and showed Delibes's gift for dance rhythm.
entries.synopsis: A carnival in Venice: Harlequin pursues Columbine through dances of Pierrot, Harlequin, the butterfly and the revelers, ending in a general celebration.

entries.title: La Bayadère
entries.dates: Premiered 4 February 1877, Mariinsky Theatre, St Petersburg
entries.history: Petipa's exotic ballet to Minkus's score at the Mariinsky Theatre, inspired by 19th-century French travel writing about India. Its 'Kingdom of the Shades' — 32 women in white tutus descending a ramp — became the most iconic image of classical ballet.
entries.synopsis: The warrior Nikiya loves the nobleman Solor, who is betrothed to the Rajah's daughter Gamzatti. Nikiya is killed by a snake hidden in Gamzatti's basket; Solor's vision of her spirit in the Kingdom of the Shades is the ballet's famous white act.

image.credit: Unknown photographer of the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre. St. Petersburg, Russian Empire

entries.title: Swan Lake
entries.dates: Premiered 4 March 1877, Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow; landmark revival 26 February 1895, Mariinsky Theatre
entries.history: Tchaikovsky's first ballet, initially choreographed by Julius Reisinger for the Bolshoi. The 1895 Mariinsky production by Petipa and Ivanov, with Pierina Legnani as Odette/Odile, created the version now standard worldwide.
entries.synopsis: Prince Siegfried is to choose a bride at his coming-of-age ball; he falls in love with Odette, queen of the swans cursed by the sorcerer Rothbart. At the ball he is deceived by Rothbart's daughter Odile, breaks his vow, and only Odette's forgiveness — or their joint death — can break the spell.

entries.title: Raymonda
entries.dates: Premiered 1898, Mariinsky Theatre, St Petersburg
entries.history: Petipa's last great narrative ballet at the Mariinsky, to music by Alexander Glazunov (his ballet score). It combined Hungarian and Slavic folk dances with classical display and was a vehicle for the Mariinsky's stars.
entries.synopsis: The chivalric Raymonda dreams she is abducted by the Saracen chief Abderahman; her fiancé Jean de Brienne rescues her. The ballet alternates Hungarian festival scenes with the dream ballet of the White Lady.

image.credit: Unknown photographer of the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre. St. Petersburg, Russian Empire.

entries.title: The Sleeping Beauty
entries.dates: Premiered 15 January 1890, Mariinsky Theatre, St Petersburg
entries.history: Petipa's grandest ballet, commissioned by the director of the Imperial Theatres Ivan Vsevolozhsky, to Tchaikovsky's magnificent score and a scenario by Petipa and Marius... based on Perrault's tale. Carlotta Brianza danced Aurora. It epitomises the classical style: the Rose Adagio, the garland waltz, Carabosse.
entries.synopsis: The wicked fairy Carabosse curses the infant Princess Aurora to prick her finger and die; the Lilac Fairy softens the curse to a hundred-year sleep. Prince Désiré awakens her with a kiss and they marry in a grand divertissement of fairy-tale characters.

image.credit: Unknown〔The original uploader was Mrlopez2681 at English Wikipedia.〕
image.commonsTitle: File:Sleeping Beauty -Marie Petipa as the Lilac Fairy & Lyubov Vishnevskaya as an Attendant -1890.JPG

entries.title: The Nutcracker
entries.dates: Premiered 18 December 1892, Mariinsky Theatre, St Petersburg
entries.history: The last of Tchaikovsky's three ballets, choreographed by Lev Ivanov while Petipa was ill, to Tchaikovsky's score and a scenario after Hoffmann's tale. Though coolly received at first, it became the world's most popular Christmas ballet.
entries.synopsis: On Christmas Eve, Clara receives a nutcracker doll from Drosselmeyer; at midnight the toys come to life, the Nutcracker becomes a prince and takes her to the Land of Sweets, where she dances with the Sugar Plum Fairy.

image.commonsTitle: File:Nutcracker Scene from Act I -Sergei Legat as Nutcracker 1892 cropped.jpg

entries.title: The Firebird
entries.dates: Premiered 25 June 1910, Paris Opéra (Palais Garnier)
entries.history: The first triumph of Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, choreographed by Michel Fokine to Igor Stravinsky's blazing debut score, with décor by Alexandre Golovin and Léon Bakst and Tamara Karsavina as the Firebird. It announced the Ballets Russes to Paris.
entries.synopsis: The sorcerer Kastchei holds the magical Firebird and maidens captive. Prince Ivan captures the Firebird, who gives him a magic feather; with it he defeats Kastchei, frees the princesses and marries the Tsarevna.

image.commonsTitle: File:Tamara Karsavina Michel Fokine The Firebird 1910.jpg

entries.title: Scheherazade
entries.dates: Premiered 4 June 1910, Paris Opéra (Palais Garnier)
entries.history: Fokine's Ballets Russes production to Rimsky-Korsakov's symphonic suite, with sumptuous oriental décor by Bakst. Its sensual choreography caused a scandal and defined the company's exotic style.
entries.synopsis: The Sultan Shahriyar, betrayed by his wife, vows to execute a new bride each night. Scheherazade saves herself and the vizier's daughter Zobeida by telling tales across a thousand and one nights, until the Sultan relents.

image.credit: Unknown photographer for the Ballets Russes.

entries.title: Petrushka
entries.dates: Premiered 13 June 1911, Théâtre du Châtelet, Paris
entries.history: Fokine's Ballets Russes ballet to Stravinsky's score, with décor by Benois, libretto by Alexandre Benois. Nijinsky's portrayal of the lovelorn puppet made it legendary; the Shrovetide fair scenes remain a landmark of modern ballet.
entries.synopsis: At a St Petersburg fair, the showman animates three puppets — Petrushka, the Ballerina and the Moor. Petrushka's despair and his murder by the Moor in a jealous rage are the ballet's tragic heart.

image.credit: Unknown photographer for the Ballets Russes.

entries.title: L'Après-midi d'un faune
entries.dates: Premiered 29 May 1912, Théâtre du Châtelet, Paris
entries.history: Nijinsky's own choreographic debut for the Ballets Russes, to Debussy's Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune, with décor by Bakst. His overtly sexual solo caused a scandal in Paris; the ballet is a cornerstone of modern dance.
entries.synopsis: A faun lolls in the forest, pursued by nymphs; he takes one by force, then fantasises alone on a scarf she leaves behind, as Debussy's music drifts away.

image.commonsTitle: File:Faun left, dancing maenad right, from Nijinsky "L'Apres-midi d'un Faune", 1912.jpg

entries.title: The Rite of Spring
entries.dates: Premiered 29 May 1913, Théâtre du Châtelet, Paris
entries.history: Nijinsky's Ballets Russes choreography to Stravinsky's revolutionary score caused a riot at the premiere — the most famous scandal in ballet history. Its pagan sacrifice ritual and pounding rhythms changed the course of 20th-century music and dance.
entries.synopsis: A Russian tribe prepares for spring: games, rituals, the choosing of an virgin who is danced to death as a sacrifice to the god Yarilo.

image.commonsTitle: File:Le Sacre du printemps by Roerich 03.jpg

entries.title: Parade
entries.dates: Premiered 18 May 1917, Théâtre du Châtelet, Paris
entries.history: Massine's Ballets Russes 'realist' ballet with music by Erik Satie (including a typewriter and pistol shot), costumes and curtain by Picasso. Diaghilev called it the high point of the company's Paris season.
entries.synopsis: A Paris crowd watches a parade of circus performers — acrobats, a horse, a 'little American girl' — trying in vain to lure spectators into a hall; they end by eating together on stage.

image.commonsTitle: File:Erik Satie - "Parade" - Ballet - Thème de Jean Cocteau - Rideau, - Décor et costumes de Picasso - Chorégraphie de Massine (manuscrit autographe) - btv1b10462747r (01 of 57).jpg

entries.title: Marie Taglioni
entries.history: The first great ballerina en pointe and the embodiment of the Romantic style. Daughter of choreographer Filippo Taglioni, she made her debut at the Paris Opéra and created the title role of La Sylphide (1832), wearing the first tulle tutu. Her ethereal 'sylphide' image defined ballet for a generation.

entries.title: Carlotta Grisi
entries.history: The Italian ballerina who created Giselle (1841) and danced in Pas de Quatre (1845). Gautier loved her and wrote the Giselle libretto around her; she was famed for the 'moonlit' second act of Giselle, where she seemed to float.

image.credit: John Henry Robinson (1796–1871), after  Alfred Edward Chalon (1780-1860)
image.commonsTitle: File:Carlotta Grisi in the title role of Giselle, 1842.jpg

entries.title: Fanny Elssler
entries.history: The Viennese 'pagan' dancer, rival of Taglioni, who conquered Paris in 1834. Known for fiery character roles and the cachucha, she toured America in 1840 and was the first ballerina to win a triumph in the New World.

entries.title: Fanny Cerrito
entries.history: The London-based star of the 1840s, associated with Perrot's ballets at Her Majesty's Theatre — she danced in Pas de Quatre (1845) and was celebrated for her pirouettes and the 'Cerrito' style of quick, precise footwork.

image.commonsTitle: File:Lithograph by Haguntal of Fanny Cerrito, 1844.JPG

entries.title: Lucile Grahn
entries.history: The Danish ballerina, pupil of Bournonville, who danced in the original Pas de Quatre (1845). She was the last of the four great Romantic ballerinas to perform, touring until the 1880s.

entries.title: Jules Perrot
entries.history: The greatest male dancer of the Romantic era and a major choreographer. He created Giselle with Coralli (1841) and produced Esmeralda, Pas de Quatre and Le Corsaire in London, where he was ballet master at Her Majesty's Theatre from 1842 to 1852.

entries.title: Pierina Legnani
entries.history: The Italian prima ballerina of the Mariinsky Theatre. In the 1895 revival of Swan Lake she danced both Odette and Odile and performed 32 consecutive fouettés in the Black Swan coda — a feat never equalled on that stage. She also created roles in Petipa's ballets.

entries.title: Anna Pavlova
entries.history: The Russian ballerina who made ballet world-famous. A protégée of Diaghilev's Ballets Russes (1909–10), she created The Dying Swan (Fokine, 1905) and toured the globe for 20 years, bringing Swan Lake and Giselle to audiences who had never seen ballet.

image.credit: Photography studio of the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre. St. Petersburg, Russian Empire.

entries.title: Vaslav Nijinsky
entries.history: The Ballets Russes' greatest male dancer and a revolutionary choreographer. He created Petrushka (1911), L'Après-midi d'un faune (1912) and The Rite of Spring (1913), whose 1912 premiere scandal shocked Paris. Dismissed by Diaghilev in 1913, he spent his last decades in mental institutions.

entries.title: Mathilde Kschessinska
entries.history: Prima ballerina of the Mariinsky Theatre and mistress of Tsarevich Nicholas (later Nicholas II). She created roles in Petipa's ballets at the Mariinsky and, after the Revolution, taught ballet in Paris.

image.commonsTitle: File:Mathilde Kschessinska in the winter garden.jpg

entries.title: Sergei Diaghilev
entries.history: Founder and impresario of the Ballets Russes (1909–1929), the company that transformed ballet in the 20th century. From Paris he commissioned Stravinsky, Debussy, Ravel, Picasso, Matisse and Nijinsky, producing The Firebird, Petrushka, The Rite of Spring and Parade. He died in Venice in 1929; the company dissolved with him.
sources: Oxford Reference — Grove Dance, Ballets Russes

image.credit: George Grantham Bain Collection (Library of Congress)

entries.title: Ivan Vsevolozhsky
entries.history: Director of the Imperial Theatres in St Petersburg (1881–1898) and a playwright himself. He commissioned the great Petipa–Tchaikovsky ballets — The Sleeping Beauty (1890), The Nutcracker (1892) and the 1895 Swan Lake — and staged the 1877 premiere of Swan Lake at the Bolshoi.
sources: Oxford Reference — Grove Dance, Imperial Theatres

image.commonsTitle: File:Ivan Vsevolozhsky, Dmitry von Benсkendorff, c. 1902, Historical Museum, Moscow И II 7750.jpg

entries.title: Marius Petipa
entries.history: The French-born choreographer who created the classical style in Russia. Ballet master at the Mariinsky from 1847, he choreographed more than 50 ballets — La Bayadère, Don Quixote, Swan Lake (1895), The Sleeping Beauty, Raymonda, The Nutcracker — and set the pattern of the full-length Russian ballet.

entries.title: Michel Fokine
entries.history: Choreographer of the early Ballets Russes and author of its 1914 'five principles', which broke with Petipa's classical conventions. He created The Firebird (1910), Scheherazade (1910), Petrushka (1911) and The Dying Swan (1905) for Anna Pavlova.

entries.title: Léonide Massine
entries.history: The Ballets Russes' great character choreographer after Nijinsky. He created Parade (1917, with Picasso and Satie), The Three-Cornered Hat (1919) and many works blending folk dance, commedia dell'arte and modern design.

image.commonsTitle: File:Massine, Leonide (1895-1979) - 1914 - Ritratto da Leon Bakst.jpg

entries.title: August Bournonville
entries.history: The Danish master who preserved the Romantic style in Copenhagen. Director of the Royal Danish Ballet, he created his own La Sylphide (1836) — the version still danced today — plus Napoli and A Folk Tale, and trained generations of Danish dancers.

entries.title: Salle Le Peletier (Paris Opéra)
entries.dates: In use 1821–1873 (burned down 1873)
entries.history: The home of the Paris Opéra from 1821 until it burned in 1873. It was here that Romantic ballet reached its peak: La Sylphide (1832), Giselle (1841), Le Corsaire (1856), Coppélia (1870) and Le Carnaval (1873) all premiered on this stage.

image.commonsTitle: File:Vue de la nouvelle salle de l'Opéra prise de la rue de Provence - NYPL Digital Collections.jpg

entries.title: Palais Garnier (Paris Opéra)
entries.dates: Opened 5 January 1875
entries.history: The Paris Opéra's home since 1875, designed by Charles Garnier in the lavish Napoleon III style — gilded ceilings, a grand staircase and Chagall's ceiling painting. It hosted the Ballets Russes premieres of The Firebird and Scheherazade in 1910.

entries.title: Mariinsky Theatre, St Petersburg
entries.dates: Current building opened 1860 (architect Alberto Cavos)
entries.history: The premier stage of Russian classical ballet. The present theatre opened in 1860 and was where Petipa created La Bayadère, The Sleeping Beauty, Raymonda, The Nutcracker and the 1895 Swan Lake. Today it is home to the Mariinsky Ballet.

entries.title: Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow
entries.dates: Opened 1825; rebuilt after the 1853 fire, reopened 1856 (architect Alberto Cavos)
entries.history: Moscow's great opera and ballet house. The original theatre opened in 1825 and was rebuilt by Cavos after a fire, reopening in 1856. It premiered Petipa's The Daughter of Pharaoh and Don Quixote and the first Swan Lake in 1877.

entries.title: Her Majesty's Theatre, London
entries.dates: Opened 1705; rebuilt 1821; demolished 1892
entries.history: The London home of Italian opera and ballet in the 19th century, on the Haymarket. Jules Perrot was ballet master here from 1842; La Esmeralda (1844) and Pas de Quatre (1845) premiered on this stage.
sources: Oxford Reference — Grove Dance, London ballet

image.commonsTitle: File:Scene from the new ballet Rosida, at her Majesty's Theatre - estampe - btv1b53117835q (2 of 2).jpg

entries.title: Théâtre du Châtelet, Paris
entries.dates: Opened 1862
entries.history: The modern Paris theatre on the Place du Châtelet that became the home of Diaghilev's Ballets Russes from 1911: Petrushka (1911), L'Après-midi d'un faune (1912), The Rite of Spring (1913) and Parade (1917) all premiered here.

image.commonsTitle: File:Théâtre Lyrique (Place du Châtelet) 1862 - Huebner 1990 plate8.jpg

entries.title: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
entries.history: The Russian composer of the three great classical ballets — Swan Lake (1877), The Sleeping Beauty (1890) and The Nutcracker (1892) — which remain the core of the world's ballet repertoire. His ballet scores pioneered symphonic storytelling in dance.

entries.title: Léo Delibes
entries.history: The French composer who made ballet music an art: Coppélia (1870), the ballet Le Carnaval (1873) and Sylvia (1876). His scores are prized for grace, colour and perfect dance rhythm.

entries.title: Ludwig Minkus
entries.history: The Austrian-born composer of the Imperial Ballet in St Petersburg, who wrote the scores for Petipa's Don Quixote (1869) and La Bayadère (1877), among many others. His music is brilliant, danceable and full of exotic colour.

entries.title: Adolphe Adam
entries.history: The French composer of Giselle (1841) and Le Corsaire (1856) — the two Romantic ballets that defined the Paris Opéra. Giselle's score, with its famous Wilis leitmotif, was the first ballet music written specifically for the stage.

entries.title: Igor Stravinsky
entries.history: The composer of the Ballets Russes' three revolutionary scores — The Firebird (1910), Petrushka (1911) and The Rite of Spring (1913) — which changed the sound of the 20th century. The Rite's premiere riot is the most famous scandal in music history.

image.commonsTitle: File:Igor Stravinsky et Claude Debussy - btv1b7002391c.jpg

entries.title: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov
entries.history: The Russian master of orchestral colour whose symphonic suite Scheherazade (1888) provided the score for Fokine's 1910 Ballets Russes ballet. He also composed The Snow Maiden and many operas.
